name: Pore strips

card.summary: Adhesive strips that lift surface blackhead plugs from the nose and face; the effect is temporary and there is little clinical research.
card.note: Wikipedia notes they can damage skin by tearing it and leaving pores wide open.

quick.overview:
Pore strips are adhesive strips pressed onto damp skin, usually the nose, and peeled off to pull out the surface of blackheads. They are sold over the counter for cosmetic pore clearing.

Blackheads are clogged follicles, and the plug returns as the follicle refills with sebum and keratin. Published research on the strips is scarce; one study used them as a sampling tool for skin bacteria.
quick.mechanism: The adhesive bonds to the surface of the plug in an open comedo and lifts it as the strip is removed. Wikipedia says the strips can lift blackheads over an area.
quick.risks: Wikipedia says pore strips can damage skin, leaving pores wide open and tearing away surrounding skin. No other safety data were found in the sources reviewed.

lead: Pore strips are adhesive strips applied to the skin, most often the nose, and peeled off to remove the surface of blackheads and sebum plugs. They are a consumer cosmetic product [1].

A blackhead is an open comedo, a hair follicle plugged with keratin and sebum whose dark colour comes from oxidation rather than dirt [1]. Wikipedia states that commercial pore strips can lift blackheads across an area, but can damage skin by leaving pores wide open and tearing away surrounding skin [1].

Clinical research on pore strips as a treatment is limited. In the sources reviewed they appear mainly as a sampling method: a 2018 study compared surface swabs, pore strips and cyanoacrylate glue to sample the follicular microbiome in 20 volunteers [2].
infobox: Open comedones (blackheads), usually on the nose

paras: Pore strips are typically moistened onto the skin, left to dry and peeled off. The plug lifted is the surface portion of the comedo. Blackheads form when keratin and sebum block a follicle open to air [1].

Wikipedia reports that strips lift blackheads but can damage skin, leaving pores wide open and tearing surrounding skin [1]. It lists other approaches, such as dermatologist extraction and retinoids, which it says have some research support, and notes that squeezing can raise the risk of infection and scarring [1].

No studies found testing pore strips as an acne or blackhead treatment. A 2018 study in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology used pore strips among methods to sample the follicular microbiome, with implications for acne research [2].
Pore strips are mentioned in body-care and skin-routine discussions as a quick, temporary blackhead remover. No community material is cited here.

refs.title: Isolation and Identification of the Follicular Microbiome: Implications for Acne Research
